ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Ammonia is not the diagnosis

A patient with cirrhosis has an elevated ammonia level during a routine visit but is alert, oriented and functioning normally. A trainee proposes diagnosing overt hepatic encephalopathy solely from this result. Which response is most accurate?

  1. Ammonia elevation alone does not establish overt hepatic encephalopathy
  2. Every elevated ammonia result proves overt HE
  3. Ammonia concentration precisely determines the clinical grade
  4. Normal cognition should be ignored if ammonia is high
  5. A single ammonia result rules out all other brain disorders
Answer and explanation

Ammonia elevation alone does not establish overt hepatic encephalopathy

HE is a clinical diagnosis requiring assessment of cognition and alternative causes.

Option explanations

Ammonia elevation alone does not establish overt hepatic encephalopathy: HE is a clinical diagnosis requiring assessment of cognition and alternative causes.

Every elevated ammonia result proves overt HE: An isolated elevation is insufficient.

Ammonia concentration precisely determines the clinical grade: Ammonia does not reliably grade clinical severity by itself.

Normal cognition should be ignored if ammonia is high: The clinical examination is central.

A single ammonia result rules out all other brain disorders: It cannot exclude alternative diagnoses.
